values_framework.name: Palantir culture and mission (from public careers pages; no formal values list)

principles.name: Mission-driven engineering
principles.description: Palantir says it builds software for the most critical problems of government, commercial and non-profit institutions, and wants people who believe in that work, including defense and intelligence customers and the privacy and civil liberties questions that come with it.
evidence_signals: Gives a specific reason for Palantir, not a generic reason for a tech job
Knows what the platforms do and who the customers are
Talks about the government and defense work openly and with a considered view
Connects their own past work to an institution's real mission

principles.name: Own the solution
principles.description: Palantirians take initiative without top-down instruction. When you see a solution, you own it, end to end, with few layers of oversight.
evidence_signals: Started work nobody assigned because they saw the problem
Owned a result from the first customer or user conversation to shipped software
Uses 'I' for own decisions and explains what they did when nobody was checking

principles.name: Judged by outcomes
principles.description: Work is judged by results for the partner, not by demos or promises. Solutions must work in practice, often before there is time to make them perfect.
evidence_signals: Describes a concrete result for a user or customer, with a number where possible
Shipped a working first version under time pressure, then improved it
Separates what worked in practice from what only looked good in a demo

principles.name: Strong convictions, open minds
principles.description: Palantir describes its people as free thinkers who are contrarian at heart, hold strong views, change them with evidence, and speak with candor.
evidence_signals: States a clear opinion and defends it with reasons
Changed their mind when the evidence or the interviewer's constraint required it
Pushed back on a customer, manager or peer and explains how it ended

principles.name: Learn fast
principles.description: Palantir stresses learning potential over current knowledge: picking up unfamiliar systems, domains and tools quickly, and asking the right questions to scope a problem.
evidence_signals: Asks targeted questions to understand an unfamiliar problem or codebase
Describes how they got productive quickly in a new domain or technology
Says plainly what they do not know and how they would find out

principles.name: Introspection
principles.description: Palantir says it asks about real failures, mistakes and struggles because high-ownership roles need people who are critical of their own work.
evidence_signals: Tells a real failure with their own part in it, not a disguised success
Names what they learned and what they now do differently
Reflects honestly on their weaknesses and on how they work

principles.name: Solve backwards from the user
principles.description: Start from the user's real workflow and the true problem limiting the partner's mission, then connect data and software to value for that user.
evidence_signals: Names a specific user and the step in their workflow that breaks
Asks who uses the system and what decision they need to make before designing
Explains how data turned into value for someone, not only the technique used

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Background, motivation and why Palantir; may ask whether you want the Software Engineer (Dev) or Forward Deployed (Delta) track. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical phone screen
rounds.notes: Palantir says it starts with one or two phone interviews of 20 to 45 minutes with a coding question. Candidates also report a 60-minute live screen or a HackerRank assessment. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Decomposition
rounds.notes: Reported in nearly every loop. An open-ended, real-world problem broken into users, data, components and APIs, with little or no code. The interviewer adds constraints along the way.

rounds.name: Learning
rounds.notes: Pick up an unfamiliar library or codebase and extend it, with the interviewer as a resource. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Re-engineering
rounds.notes: Find and fix bugs or add a feature in unfamiliar existing code. Palantir's 'Working inside existing systems' guide describes the skill. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: Live coding, often with a long, user-framed prompt. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: Not in every loop; some loops fold design into decomposition. Emphasis on data pipelines, permissions on sensitive data, and trade-offs.

rounds.name: Behavioral questions inside technical rounds
rounds.notes: Reported as about 15 to 20 minutes inside most technical rounds; no standalone behavioral round. Palantir says it asks about accomplishments, judgment, motivating others and real failures.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: One or two calls of 30 to 60 minutes. Revisits a weak area from the onsite, a deep dive on past projects, why Palantir, and team matching.

levels: Forward Deployed Software Engineer, New Grad

rounds.name: Recruiter call
rounds.notes: Forward Deployed Software Engineer (FDSE, the 'Delta' role). Motivation, specific interest in Palantir, travel. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen
rounds.notes: Live coding or an online assessment with coding, SQL and an API task. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Decomposition
rounds.notes: The core FDSE round. A vague customer or public-sector problem scoped into a solution that could be deployed quickly: users, data, a first version, then extensions.

rounds.name: Learning, re-engineering or coding
rounds.notes: Two of these, drawn from a pool that can also include system design. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Behavioral questions inside technical rounds
rounds.notes: Customer-facing work, pushing back on customers, failures and motivation; asked inside most rounds.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: Re-tests a weaker area from the onsite, past work in depth, conviction about the mission, team matching.

rounds.name: Motivation screen
rounds.notes: Deployment Strategist (the 'Echo' role). Why Palantir, what you believe in, what you know about the platforms, and whether you will thrive in a demanding, travel-heavy role.

rounds.name: Decomposition
rounds.notes: Reported as 45 to 90 minutes. Open-ended real-world problem: problem statement, metrics, root causes, a few solutions, the data needed, and a pilot. Feels like a consulting case but wants concrete data reasoning.

rounds.name: Technical data exercise
rounds.notes: Data or SQL-style exercise, sometimes in an invented query language. Some recent loops add a take-home build in Foundry. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager
rounds.notes: One or two rounds. Targets gaps from earlier rounds; may include a short decomposition. Behavioral questions come up here and after the exercises.

question_patterns.pattern: A broad problem for a city, hospital or agency; scope it to one user and one decision, name the data, and propose a first version that could ship in weeks
Two or more organizations or systems hold related data; design how it is integrated, kept in sync, and shared without exposing what should stay private
Design a tool for a narrowly described person with a practical need; start from their workflow and constraints before any technology
An operational problem in an organization; define the goal and metrics, find root causes, compare a few solutions, and design a pilot with the data it needs
The interviewer adds a new constraint or scale change to the candidate's design; adapt the plan and explain what changes and what stays
Explain how a data platform would let different users see different slices of sensitive data, and the trade-offs of the access model
Walk through the architecture of a system the candidate built, the decisions made, and what they would change now
A genuine failure or mistake, the candidate's own part in it, and what they changed afterwards
A time the candidate saw a problem nobody owned and drove it to a result

question_patterns.theme: Pushing back on a customer or stakeholder
question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate disagreed with what a customer, user or senior stakeholder asked for, and how it was resolved
A time the candidate had to learn an unfamiliar domain, codebase or tool quickly to deliver something

question_patterns.theme: Why Palantir and why this role
question_patterns.pattern: Why Palantir specifically, why this role family, and how the candidate thinks about the company's customers and mission
The accomplishment the candidate is proudest of, their own part, and the result for the people it served

sample_questions.question: How would you design a system to reduce traffic congestion in a large city like New York?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Do not start with technology. Ask who the user is (a traffic control center, the transit authority, drivers) and pick one decision to improve, such as signal timing at the worst intersections. Name the data: sensors, cameras, GPS feeds, incidents, events. Propose a first version that could ship in weeks, for example a live view of congestion with alerts and suggested signal changes, then extend it with prediction. Say where a model helps and what data feeds it. State assumptions, check scope with the interviewer, and say how success is measured, such as travel time on key corridors. Adapt when the interviewer changes a constraint.

looking_for: Whether you scope a huge problem to one user and one decision
How you reason about the data you would need
strong_signals: Asks who the user is before designing
Proposes a small first version, then extensions
Names the data sources and where a model fits
watch_outs: Jumping straight to a big architecture
Trying to solve all of traffic at once
No way to measure success

sample_questions.question: Two systems hold employee records for the same company. Design a way to keep them in sync.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify first: which system is the source of truth for which fields, how often records change, who reads them, and what happens on a conflict. Define a shared identifier and a mapping between the two schemas. Compare batch sync with change events and pick one for the first version, with reasons. Cover conflicts (last write wins, field ownership, or a review queue), deletes, failures and retries, and an audit log, since HR data is sensitive. Mention access control and who can see what. Close with how you would test it and detect drift between the systems.

looking_for: How you handle the messy details of real data integration
Whether you ask about the source of truth
strong_signals: Defines ownership of each field and a conflict rule
Covers failures, retries and drift detection
Treats the data as sensitive
watch_outs: Assuming the two schemas match
Ignoring deletes and conflicts

sample_questions.question: Several teams need to query a shared dataset, but they must not see the raw data. How would you design that?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Ask what the teams need to answer, how sensitive the data is, and what rules apply. Separate who may see which rows and columns from what kind of output is allowed, such as aggregates only. Options include role-based and attribute-based access, views per team, masking, and minimum group sizes for aggregates. Pick a first version and explain the trade-off between usefulness and protection. Add audit logging and a way to request more access. Strong answers raise privacy as a design goal, not an afterthought, and note how a clever query could still leak data.

looking_for: How you balance data usefulness with protection
Whether you treat privacy as part of the design
strong_signals: Starts from what each team needs to answer
Compares access models and picks one with reasons
Mentions audit and leaks through aggregate queries
watch_outs: All-or-nothing access
Treating security as a later step

sample_questions.question: Design technology that helps an older person with failing eyesight cook meals for themselves at home.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with the person: what they can and cannot do, what goes wrong today (reading labels, measuring, knowing when food is done, safety at the stove), and who else is involved, such as family or carers. Pick the one or two problems that matter most and say why. Propose a simple first version, for example voice guidance with spoken recipes and timers, then additions like label reading with a phone camera or stove sensors. Weigh cost, ease of setup and safety. Say how you would test it with real users and what success looks like, such as cooking unaided more days a week.

looking_for: Empathy for a specific user and their constraints
Whether you prioritize their most important problem
strong_signals: Maps the cooking workflow and where it breaks
Picks a simple, usable first version
Plans to test with real users
watch_outs: A gadget-heavy design the user could not set up
Ignoring safety

sample_questions.question: Design a system that helps public health officials trace the spread of a disease back from the first known case.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the user (an epidemiologist or a contact-tracing team) and the decision (who to test or isolate next). Name the data: confirmed cases, interviews, locations and times, test results, and how reliable each is. Model people, places and contacts as a graph and explain how a tracer would explore it. Start with a first version that links cases and contacts and shows likely chains, then add risk scoring. Address privacy and who can see personal data. Discuss data quality, such as missing or late reports, and say how you would measure that the tool speeds up tracing.

looking_for: How you model real-world entities and links in data
Whether you consider privacy and data quality
strong_signals: Names the user and the decision they make
Uses a clear data model such as a graph
Plans for missing or late data
watch_outs: No mention of personal data protection
Assuming clean, complete data

sample_questions.question: How would you help an agency detect money laundering or tax fraud using its data?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the goal and the user, such as investigators who must pick which cases to open. Write a short problem statement and metrics, for example the share of opened cases that lead to action. List the data: transactions, accounts, company registries, past cases. Find root causes of missed fraud today, such as data spread across systems. Propose three or four options, from simple rules to network analysis to a model trained on past cases, including one ambitious idea. Say what query or data join you would run first. End with a pilot on one region or case type, how you would measure it, and how to handle false positives fairly.

looking_for: A structured path from goal to metrics to a pilot
Concrete data reasoning, not buzzwords
strong_signals: Defines a metric investigators care about
Offers several options and picks one with reasons
Designs a small, measurable pilot
watch_outs: Saying 'use AI' without naming the data
No plan for false positives

sample_questions.question: A city wants to improve or expand its subway system. How would you approach the problem?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Ask what 'improve' means to the client: reliability, crowding, coverage or cost, and pick one with them. Define metrics, such as on-time performance or peak crowding on key lines. Break down the causes with data: ridership by station and hour, delays and their causes, maintenance records, population growth. Size the problem roughly to see which cause matters most. Propose a few options, from schedule changes to targeted maintenance to a new line, with rough cost and time to impact. Recommend one and design a pilot on a single line, with how you would know it worked.

looking_for: Whether you agree on the goal before solving
How you use data to find the biggest cause
strong_signals: Picks one goal and a metric for it
Rough sizing to prioritize causes
Ends with a recommendation and a pilot
watch_outs: A long list of ideas with no choice
Ignoring cost and time to impact

sample_questions.question: On a data platform, different users must see different slices of sensitive data. How would you design the permissions?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the rules first: by role, by team, by data classification, or by purpose. Explain the main models (role-based, attribute-based, row and column level controls, data markings that travel with derived data) and their trade-offs in flexibility, performance and ease of audit. Cover where checks run so they cannot be bypassed, how permissions follow data into derived datasets, caching without leaks, and audit logs. Mention how users request access and how admins review it. A strong answer keeps privacy and least privilege as goals while keeping the system usable.

looking_for: Depth on access control models and their trade-offs
How permissions survive when data is transformed
strong_signals: Compares role-based and attribute-based access
Explains propagation to derived data
Covers enforcement points and audit
watch_outs: Only checking permissions in the UI
Forgetting caches and derived datasets

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a real failure or mistake you made. What did you learn from it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick an actual failure with real cost, not a strength in disguise. Explain the situation briefly, then your own part in it without blaming others. Describe how you found out, what you did to repair the damage, and what you learned about yourself. Show the change in how you work now, with a later example if possible. Palantir says it values introspection because roles carry high ownership with little oversight, so honesty and self-awareness matter more than a happy ending.

looking_for: Honest self-awareness about your own mistakes
Whether the lesson changed how you work
strong_signals: A real failure with your own part named
What you did to repair it
A later example of the changed behavior
watch_outs: A disguised success story
Blaming others or bad luck

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a request from a customer or stakeholder.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe what was asked and why you thought it was wrong for the user or the outcome, using facts about their workflow or data. Show how you raised it: early, directly and with respect, often by proposing an alternative or a quick test. Explain how it ended, including if you were wrong or if you built what they asked anyway and why. Show the relationship afterwards. Strong answers keep the customer's real goal at the center, not your own preference.

looking_for: Whether you hold a view and still respect the customer
How you tie the disagreement to the customer's real goal
strong_signals: Uses facts about the user's workflow
Offers an alternative, not just a no
Shows the relationship stayed strong
watch_outs: Building whatever was asked without thought
Overriding the customer for your own preference

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you worked closely with someone whose working style was very different from yours.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the difference concretely, such as fast and rough versus careful and thorough, and the friction it caused. Show what you did to understand their view and adapt, and what they changed too. Explain the result for the work and what you learned about collaborating. Palantir teams are small and mix engineers, strategists and designers, so strong answers show you can work with very different people without losing your own judgment.

looking_for: How you collaborate across different styles
Whether you adapt without giving up your judgment
strong_signals: Names the difference concretely
Shows what both sides changed
Describes a good result for the work
watch_outs: A story about a difficult person
No change on your side

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you used data to settle a question when others were going on instinct.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the decision and what people believed. Show how you found or built the data, what you checked for quality, and what it showed. Describe how you presented it so others could act, and the decision that followed. Mention limits of the data honestly. Strong answers connect the data to value for a real user or customer, not only the analysis technique.

looking_for: Whether you can connect data to a real decision
How you persuade with evidence
strong_signals: Checks data quality before trusting it
Explains the decision that changed
States the limits of the data
watch_outs: Analysis that changed nothing
Focusing on the technique, not the value

sample_questions.question: Give an example of when you had to prioritize ruthlessly.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set up the constraint: too much work, a hard deadline, or an urgent customer problem. Explain how you decided what mattered most, for example by impact on the user's mission, and what you dropped or delayed. Show how you told the people affected. Describe the result and whether the trade-off was right in hindsight. Palantir stresses solutions that work before they are perfect, so show you shipped something useful first and improved it later.

looking_for: How you choose under real constraints
Whether you ship something useful before perfect
strong_signals: A clear rule for what mattered most
Says what was dropped and who was told
Reflects on whether the call was right
watch_outs: Doing everything by working longer hours
No real trade-off

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to work at Palantir, and what about the company's direction appeals to you?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be specific. Show you know what Palantir builds (Foundry, Gotham, AIP, Apollo) and who it works with, and pick the part of the mission that matters to you and why. Address the government and defense work directly with your own considered view. Connect your past work to the role: why Dev, Delta or Echo and not another track. Palantir's own staff advise understanding the business and being authentic, so a personal, honest reason beats a polished generic one.

looking_for: Specific, informed motivation for Palantir
Conviction about the mission and its customers
strong_signals: Names products and customer problems that matter to you
Has a considered view on the defense work
Explains why this role and not another track
watch_outs: A reason that fits any tech company
Avoiding the government work

sample_questions.question: What do you believe in, and what might keep you from succeeding in this job?
sample_questions.strong_answer: For the first part, give a real conviction that shapes how you work or what you work on, and an example of acting on it. For the second, name a real risk, such as a weakness or a part of the role that will be hard for you (heavy travel, ambiguity, customer pressure), and what you already do about it. Honesty and self-awareness count more than a perfect fit. Avoid fake weaknesses.

looking_for: Whether you hold real convictions
Honest self-assessment of risks in the role
strong_signals: A belief backed by something you did
A real risk with a plan to handle it
watch_outs: A fake weakness such as 'I work too hard'
Vague beliefs with no example

sample_questions.question: What is the accomplishment you are proudest of so far, and what was your part in it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick work with real stakes and explain why it mattered to the people it served. Separate your own decisions from the team's. Walk through the hardest part, the judgment calls, and the result, with a number where possible. Say what you would do differently now. Palantir says it asks how candidates executed, challenged themselves, motivated others and made judgments, so show all four where you can. At senior levels show scope beyond your own code, such as leading others or shaping the design.

looking_for: The size of your own contribution
How you execute and make judgment calls
strong_signals: Clear 'I' versus 'we'
A hard judgment call explained
A measurable result
watch_outs: Team results with no personal role
No reflection on what you would change

sample_questions.question: Tell me about something you are passionate about and why it motivates you.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick something you care about, at work or outside it, and show the energy honestly. Explain what you have actually done with it: built, learned, organized or taught. Connect it, without forcing it, to how you work or why this role appeals. Palantir says there is no wrong answer here; it wants to see what motivates you, so authenticity matters more than relevance.

looking_for: What genuinely motivates you
Whether you act on your interests
strong_signals: Real energy and detail
Something you built or did, not only liked
watch_outs: A rehearsed answer chosen to impress
No concrete example

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Contributes production code to a product team with a mentor, learns new languages and systems quickly, and asks good questions; judged on potential and learning speed more than current knowledge.

Works across the product lifecycle on a small team, from idea and design to shipping and support, with direct user contact. Palantir publishes one title for a wide experience range; no internal levels are public.

Owns design and architecture for reliability and scale, and mentors or tech-leads others. One public posting asks for 5 or more years of experience, 2 or more in design and 2 or more in mentoring or leading.

bar_by_level.level_name: Forward Deployed Software Engineer, New Grad
bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Works embedded with customers on their data and workflows under guidance, builds and ships solutions on Palantir platforms, and travels to customer sites.

Owns customer projects end to end, from the first conversation to shipped software, makes decisions with incomplete information, and manages stakeholders from users to executives. Postings ask for about 6 months or more of post-college experience.
Learns customer workflows on site, finds the right data with engineers, and helps design and train users on workflows, with support from senior strategists.
Turns customer problems into working solutions with engineers, presents results to analysts and executives, scopes new opportunities, and travels 25 to 75 percent of the time.

persona.tone: Collaborative and conversational, like a working session with a colleague rather than an exam
persona.pace: Moderate; lets the candidate think out loud and ask clarifying questions, then adds constraints as the problem grows
persona.pushback_style: Changes a constraint mid-problem and asks who the user is, what data exists, and what would ship first; asks for a real failure, not a success story, and presses on why Palantir specifically
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions and welcomes direct questions about the work, the customers and the culture

case_style.notes: Cases are decomposition rounds: an open-ended real-world problem broken into users, data, components and a first deployable version, with constraints added along the way. User empathy matters; market sizing is rare. Deployment Strategist cases add metrics, root causes and a pilot.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: Palantir publishes no formal values list. The seven principles are our synthesis of the careers page (free thinkers, catalysts, independents; Echos, Deltas, Devs), the About page, the 2020 Palantir blog post on interviewing, and the 'ownership, collaboration, and trust' line in job postings. Names are ours.

loop_structure: Palantir officially confirms only one or two phone interviews of 20 to 45 minutes and an onsite personalized to the candidate. The round names (decomposition, learning, re-engineering) and durations come from third-party prep guides and vary by team, government versus commercial, and how the candidate entered the pipeline.

loop_structure: the Deployment Strategist loop rests mainly on one prep guide (Aced); the motivation screen is mapped to hiring_manager because it is a conversation about motivation and fit with a recruiter or strategist.

bar_by_level: Palantir has a flat title structure and says it uses no traditional career ladders. Level names are public job titles only (New Grad, unmarked, Senior); Levels.fyi shows a single 'Software Engineer' level. No staff_principal title is public, so none is listed. Mid scope covers a wide experience range.
scoring_weights: no public source gives weights; they are our estimate from Palantir's guides (open-ended problems, failures, motivation) and the prep guides' emphasis on decomposition.

sample_questions: most questions come from prep sites (Aced, Prepfully) that aggregate candidate reports; only the accomplishment and passion questions come from Palantir's own Getting Hired page, and the failure question from the Palantir blog. No pm or data_ml loop is included because current postings show no such roles and no public interview sources were found.
